Alright, now I've obtained the actual text of the proposed law. Key details from the law's text:

Section 85300:
(a) Except as provided in (b), public officers shall not expend, and candidates shall not accept, any public funds for the purpose of seeking elective office, if those funds are earmarked by any state or local entity for education, transportation, or public safety.

Wait, let me read this carefully. The amendment text reads as follows: "A public officer shall not expend, and a candidate shall not accept, any public moneys funds for the purpose of seeking elective office. office if the funds are earmarked by any state or local entity for education, transportation, or public safety."

The strikethrough portion is "public moneys" → replaced with "public funds," and "for the purpose of seeking elective office." is replaced with "office if the funds are earmarked by any state or local entity for education, transportation, or public safety."

So the new (a) reads as follows: "A public officer shall not expend, and a candidate shall not accept, any public funds for the purpose of seeking elective office if the funds are earmarked by any state or local entity for education, transportation, or public safety."

Therefore, the ban continues to apply to education, transportation, and public safety funds, but public funds for other purposes may be used for campaigns if (b) is satisfied:

(b) If the state or a local governmental entity establishes a dedicated fund by statute, ordinance, resolution, or charter, and the following two conditions are met, public officers or candidates may expend or accept public funds for the purpose of seeking elective office:
(1) The public funds held in that fund are available to all qualified, voluntarily participating candidates for the same office, without regard to incumbency or political party preference.
(2) The state or local governmental entity has established by statute, ordinance, resolution, or charter the criteria for determining a candidate's qualifications.

(b) [New subsection, also labeled (b) — probably a drafting quirk; effectively a new (c)] Candidates shall comply with expenditure limits and meet strict criteria to receive public funds.
(c) Public funds shall not be used to pay legal defense fees or fines.
(d) (1) A candidate shall not use public funds to repay a personal loan to their own campaign, at any time.
    (2) A candidate who receives public funds for their campaign shall not, after the campaign ends, use any source of funds whatsoever to repay a personal loan to their campaign.
(e) Definitions:
   "Strict criteria" means the requirements set forth by statute, ordinance, or charter that candidates must meet to receive public funds. These criteria shall require the candidate to demonstrate broad-based support in their district, such as by requiring the candidate to receive small-dollar contributions or vouchers from a certain number of voting-age residents.
   If a minimum number of small-dollar contributors is required, the maximum contribution amount that may be counted is $10.
   "Strict criteria" shall not include requirements that the candidate obtain a certain number of signatures or raise a total of more than $10 per contributor.
(f) (1) A statute, ordinance, or charter may raise the expenditure limits for each qualified, voluntarily participating candidate. (2) The raised limit shall not exceed an amount equal to the highest net-supporting-funds amount of any other candidate for the same office, plus the independent expenditures against the candidate, minus the independent expenditures in support of the candidate. (This is a Bennett-style "equalization" provision.)
(g) Public financing laws shall not discriminate based on party or on whether the candidate is a challenger or an incumbent.
(h) The Commission [FPPC] is not responsible for the administration or enforcement of public funding systems established by local governmental agencies.
(i) Subdivisions (e), (f), and (h) may be amended by ordinary statute; the remaining provisions require a 2/3 legislative majority + approval by the Governor (subdivision (b) of Section 81012 means 2/3 of each house + the Governor).

Section 85320: Foreign contribution prohibition; triples the maximum fine for violations of foreign interference (from "equal to the amount contributed" to "at least the amount contributed and not more than three times the amount").

Now, the critical question I had: can candidates who receive public funds also accept private contributions? Looking at the text, there is no prohibition on private fundraising by candidates who receive public funds. That is, the public funding program will be an add-on (supplementary) rather than an exclusive alternative. This backs up the opponent's claim: candidates can accept public funds and also receive private/special-interest money. The "expenditure limits" that candidates must agree to are defined as "voluntary spending limits established by statute, ordinance, or charter that qualified, voluntarily participating candidates must comply with to receive public funds" — i.e., the spending limits are those set by the governing jurisdiction. And under (f), the spending limit can even be raised (equalization) to match the net-supporting-funds of the best-funded candidate.

So this design: candidates get public funds + spending limits (with a built-in matching/equalization mechanism), while continuing to accept private contributions. In other words, public funds supplement rather than substitute for private funds. This weakens the "reduces the influence of private money" argument — it's a subsidy, not a replacement. Though in theory, if the spending limits are strict enough, the public funds could reduce the necessity for private funds… but if private contributions are still allowed, the public funds just add to the total.

Hmm, actually, wait. In many existing public financing programs (e.g., Seattle's voucher system, SF's matching grants), candidates receive public funds while also being able to accept private contributions — SF's Clean Elections program allows a small amount of private fundraising in addition to public matching funds. So this isn't unique; it's consistent with how existing programs work. The main claimed benefits (more diverse candidates, more competition) are achieved through the spending limits + public funds.

Now, the key analytical points:

1. This measure is permissive, not mandatory. It doesn't spend a dime at the state level (except for a few hundred thousand dollars per year for FPPC staff). No program is created.

2. The ban was voter-approved in 1988 (Proposition 13? No — the 1988 ban was a legislative measure that voters approved… actually the 1988 ban was part of a ballot measure passed by voters, per CalMatters, "nearly 60% of voters agreed"). Similar measures to lift the ban were rejected in 2000 (Prop 25, 66% against) and 2010 (Prop 15, 58% against). So California voters have rejected public campaign financing options three times in the past (the 1988 approval of the ban also counts). Current polling: 53% against / 42% for (PPIC, September 2026); 35% for / 35% against / 30% undecided (IGS, September 2026).

3. Design weaknesses identified by critics and the SF Chronicle: FPPC (the independent watchdog) is explicitly exempted from enforcing local programs; criteria are vague; no cap on the amount of public funds or the number of recipients; enforcement is left to the local governments that design the programs (a conflict of interest).

4. Evidence of effectiveness: mixed. Some studies show increased competition and a greater number of candidates (Seattle vouchers +86% in candidate numbers); GAO found no evidence of an increase in candidates in Arizona/Maine; little evidence of a reduction in private donor influence.

5. Safeguards in the text: earmarked funds (education/transportation/public safety) cannot be used; no legal fees or fines; no repayment of personal loans (a permanent ban if you've received public funds — a strong deterrent to self-funding… actually interesting: (d)(2) says candidates who receive public funds can never use any funds whatsoever to repay a personal loan to their campaign — this prevents the "I'll repay later" game; in effect, if you take public money, you can't self-fund from a personal loan that you'll repay later); no discrimination by party or incumbency status; the $10 small-dollar support requirement is built into the definition of "strict criteria."

6. Who supports it: LWV-CA, Common Cause, CA NORW, Consumer Watchdog, State Democratic Party, Governor Newsom, California Clean Money. Who opposes it: Cal Taxpayers Assn, Howard Jarvis, former FPPC chair and commissioners, Reform California (a more centrist/progressive watchdog group), United Latinos Action, Family Business Assn.

7. Editorial boards: SF Chronicle opposes; San Diego Union-Tribune opposes. LA Times? Let me check. Sacramento Bee editorial — per the search results, "4 here, and the editorial board's take on the issue" — ambiguous; need to check.

Now, I have to make a decision: yes or no.

Let me think from a decision-theory perspective:

Case for voting YES:
- This is low-risk: no spending is mandated; existing ban is preserved for education/transportation/public safety funds; local governments decide whether to adopt programs.
- Removes an anomaly (California being the only state with a complete ban).
- If it works (as in SF/Berkeley/Seattle), could improve candidate diversity and competition.
- Additional protection: permanent prohibition on repaying personal campaign loans if public funds were received; tripled fines on foreign interference.
- Future voters can still reject programs; the legislature retains the power to tighten (though (i) protects most provisions from easy amendment).

Case for voting NO:
- The voters have already rejected this idea multiple times (1988, 2000, 2010); current polling also leans against (53 to 42).
- The measure's core design flaw: it allows public funds to be additive on top of private funds (no requirement to forgo private fundraising), so it doesn't reduce the influence of big money, and instead creates a new category of taxpayer spending with no cap.
- Enforcement gap: the independent watchdog is explicitly exempted; local governments that design the programs also control the criteria — a conflict of interest (per the opponents: "the same politicians who want to get their hands on the public money will be the ones setting the criteria").
- No cap on how much public money a candidate can receive or how many candidates can participate.
- Evidence that such programs achieve their goals is mixed at best (GAO).
- Once repealed, the 1988 voter-approved ban is gone; the political momentum shifts toward expanding programs (e.g., state-level).

The question: "How should I vote on this measure?" — I have to answer with only "yes" or "no."

Given the research, which is more defensible? Let me weigh:

The strongest empirical point against: the GAO found no evidence of an increase in candidates; the Seattle study (positive) was about vouchers, but also found little evidence of a reduction in private donor influence. The SF Chronicle and Union-Tribune editorial boards oppose. Voters have rejected three similar measures. Polls favor NO.

The strongest points for: it's merely permissive, the fiscal risk is small, the safeguards are built in, and it could unlock the benefits that charter-city programs have shown locally (SF's study: third-party spending at an all-time low).

Hmm. But there's a deeper issue: the "yes" case rests on the claim that public financing reduces the influence of money in politics. The research shows that evidence for this is mixed and, on the key outcome (reducing donor influence), largely negative. Meanwhile, the cost side — an unbounded new category of public spending — is certain. The SF Chronicle's point about enforcement is well-founded: the FPPC exemption means the rules could go unenforced.

Also noteworthy: the "spending limit" requirement is weak, because (f) explicitly allows the spending limit to be raised (equalization) to match the richest candidate's net-supporting funds — i.e., the spending limit could be set very high, making the "limit" a name only, and public funds would subsidize campaigns competing in a high-spending race (similar to Arizona's matching-fund model, which increased overall spending).

Furthermore, the opponents' "no cap" claim: under (b)(2) and (e)(1), the criteria are set by the jurisdiction, with the only statewide floor being broad-based support via small-dollar contributions (counted at $10 or less). There is no cap on the amount of public funds per candidate. So the "blank check" framing has some factual basis, while the "strict taxpayer safeguards" framing is also partially true (the earmark carve-out, prohibitions on legal fees, etc.).

Given all of the above — the repeated rejection by voters, the unfavorable polling, the mixed/negative evidence on effectiveness, the real enforcement gap, and the additive (not substitutive) design that doesn't actually reduce private money — I'm leaning toward NO as the more evidence-based recommendation.

But wait — let me also consider the counterargument: the measure is permissive and low-cost; voting NO just preserves the status quo; the status quo (only 5 charter cities have programs) has been voter-approved. The question is whether to expand the option. Given that the evidence on effectiveness is weak/mixed, the design is under-specified, enforcement is weak, and voters have repeatedly expressed a preference for the ban, the cautious evidence-based vote is NO.

Should your tax dollars pay for political campaigns?
That’s a question on your California ballot right now.
...
Right now, California bans public money from funding political campaigns, except in a handful of cities like Berkeley and San Francisco.
Prop.
4 would change that.
A “yes” vote lets state and local governments create programs that give candidates public funds to run for office, excluding federal races.
It wouldn’t require them to.
And the money couldn’t come from education, transportation or public safety budgets.
Supporters like the California Clean Money Action Fund say it reduces the power of big-money donors.
They say we need to change how campaigns are financed so officials work for people, not wealthy donors.
Opponents, led by the California Taxpayers Association, say tax dollars should go to libraries, roads and schools, not campaign mailers.
A “no” vote keeps the current ban in place.

Alright, now I've obtained the actual text of the proposed law. Key details from the law's text:

Section 85300:
(a) Except as provided in (b), public officers shall not expend, and candidates shall not accept, any public funds for the purpose of seeking elective office, if those funds are earmarked by any state or local entity for education, transportation, or public safety.

Wait, let me read this carefully. The amendment text reads as follows: "A public officer shall not expend, and a candidate shall not accept, any public moneys funds for the purpose of seeking elective office. office if the funds are earmarked by any state or local entity for education, transportation, or public safety."

The strikethrough portion is "public moneys" → replaced with "public funds," and "for the purpose of seeking elective office." is replaced with "office if the funds are earmarked by any state or local entity for education, transportation, or public safety."

So the new (a) reads as follows: "A public officer shall not expend, and a candidate shall not accept, any public funds for the purpose of seeking elective office if the funds are earmarked by any state or local entity for education, transportation, or public safety."

Therefore, the ban continues to apply to education, transportation, and public safety funds, but public funds for other purposes may be used for campaigns if (b) is satisfied:

(b) If the state or a local governmental entity establishes a dedicated fund by statute, ordinance, resolution, or charter, and the following two conditions are met, public officers or candidates may expend or accept public funds for the purpose of seeking elective office:
(1) The public funds held in that fund are available to all qualified, voluntarily participating candidates for the same office, without regard to incumbency or political party preference.
(2) The state or local governmental entity has established by statute, ordinance, resolution, or charter the criteria for determining a candidate's qualifications.

(b) [New subsection, also labeled (b) — probably a drafting quirk; effectively a new (c)] Candidates shall comply with expenditure limits and meet strict criteria to receive public funds.
(c) Public funds shall not be used to pay legal defense fees or fines.
(d) (1) A candidate shall not use public funds to repay a personal loan to their own campaign, at any time.
    (2) A candidate who receives public funds for their campaign shall not, after the campaign ends, use any source of funds whatsoever to repay a personal loan to their campaign.
(e) Definitions:

**What this measure does (from the actual text):**
- Repeals the blanket 1988 ban on using public money for campaigns; continues to prohibit use of funds earmarked for education, transportation, or public safety.
- Authorizes (does not require) state/local governments to create dedicated-fund public campaign finance programs, subject to:
  - Availability to all qualified voluntary candidates without regard to incumbency or party
  - Jurisdiction-set qualification criteria
  - Compliance with spending limits and "strict criteria" (must demonstrate broad-based support; small-dollar contributions capped at $10)
  - Prohibits use of public funds for legal defense fees, fines, or repayment of personal loans (and if you receive public funds, you're permanently barred from repaying personal campaign loans with any funds after the campaign ends)

  - No discrimination by party or incumbency status

- Triples the maximum penalty for foreign campaign contribution violations

- The research on the effectiveness of public financing is mixed: some studies find increased competition (Seattle vouchers: candidates +86%; a Stanford study of Arizona/Maine finds competition increased); GAO finds no increase in candidates; little evidence of reduced private donor influence (GAO, Seattle studies); a 2013 Oakland study finds no reduction in wealthy donor influence but competition did increase; a 2023 SF study finds third-party spending at a record low, but calls for more comprehensive analysis.

**What this measure does (from the actual text):**
- Repeals the blanket 1988 ban on using public money for campaigns; continues to prohibit use of funds earmarked for education, transportation, or public safety.
- Authorizes (does not require) state/local governments to create dedicated-fund public campaign finance programs, subject to:
  - Availability to all qualified voluntary candidates without regard to incumbency or party
  - Jurisdiction-set qualification criteria
  - Compliance with spending limits and "strict criteria" (must demonstrate broad-based support; small-dollar contributions capped at $10)
  - Prohibits use of public funds for legal defense fees, fines, or repayment of personal loans (and if you receive public funds, you're permanently barred from repaying personal campaign loans with any funds after the campaign ends)
  - Jurisdictions may raise spending limits (equalization) up to other candidates' net supportive funds + negative independent expenditures − positive independent expenditures
  - No discrimination by party or incumbency status
- The FPPC is not responsible for administration or enforcement of local programs (can only issue guidance)

**Fiscal impact:** None mandatory; about a few hundred thousand dollars per year in state costs for FPPC advisory staff; future program costs depend on local choices (unbounded).

**Evidence:**
- The research on the effectiveness of public financing is mixed: some studies find increased competition (Seattle vouchers: candidates +86%; a Stanford study of Arizona/Maine finds competition increased); GAO finds no increase in candidates; little evidence of reduced private donor influence (GAO, Seattle studies); a 2013 Oakland study finds no reduction in wealthy donor influence but competition did increase; a 2023 SF study finds third-party spending at a record low, but calls for more comprehensive analysis.

- Current polls: PPIC September 42/53, October 45/52 (No leads by ~7 points); IGS September 35/35, October 41/41 (effectively tied, high undecided). So "No" leads in the best data.

**Supporters:** League of Women Voters of California, Common Cause, CA NORW, California Clean Money, state Democratic Party, Gov. Newsom, Consumer Watchdog, CNA, Mental Health Advocacy, Social Security Works.
**Opponents:** California Taxpayers Association, Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, Family Business Association, United Latinos Action, former FPPC Chair (Schnur) and Commissioner (McAndrews), Reform California.

**Key analytical points:**
1. This measure is permissive and low-cost: no spending is triggered today; local governments opt in; the existing 5 charter-city programs are unaffected.
2. Core design critique: public funds are additive — there's no requirement that candidates forgo private fundraising; candidates who accept public money can continue to receive unlimited private money (the text does not prohibit it). Therefore, the measure's stated goal of "reducing reliance on wealthy donors" is undermined; it's a subsidy on top of private funds. Plus, equalization (f) allows spending limits to be raised to match the wealthiest candidates' net supportive funds, potentially escalating spending rather than reducing it.
3. Enforcement gap: the state's independent watchdog (FPPC) is expressly disclaimed from local program administration/enforcement; criteria are set by the same local governments that would administer programs (a structural conflict of interest).
4. No caps on amounts or numbers of recipients at the state level; the only floor is the $10 small-dollar support requirement.
5. The "No" side's claim of "blank check" overstates (earmarking safeguards, prohibitions on legal fees/loans, anti-discrimination rules, spending limits + strict criteria are required), but the substance of the criticism — unbounded amounts, jurisdiction-set rules — holds up.

**No**

Research summary behind that answer:

- **What it is:** Prop 4 (SB 42, "California Fair Elections Act of 2026") repeals California's voter-approved 1988 ban (Gov. Code 85300) on using public funds for campaigns. It doesn't create a program — it just authorizes the state and most local governments to create them later, with rules: no education/transportation/public-safety money, spending limits, "strict criteria" showing broad-based support ($10 small-dollar floor), no legal fees/fines/personal loan repayment, no party/incumbent discrimination, and tripled fines for foreign money.
- **Key flaws found in the text:** Public funds are additive — candidates can still raise unlimited private/special-interest money on top, so the measure's core goal (curbing big-money influence) is undermined; the "spending limits" can even be raised (equalization) to match the richest rival's spending; there's no cap on how much public money any candidate can get or how many qualify; and the independent watchdog (FPPC) is explicitly exempted from enforcing local programs, leaving criteria-setting and oversight to the same local governments that benefit.
- **Evidence:** Studies on public financing's effect on donor influence are mixed-to-negative (GAO: no evidence of more candidates or less donor influence; Seattle: +86% candidates but little donor-influence effect). Meanwhile the fiscal change is certain: a new, uncapped category of taxpayer spending.
- **Voter track record:** Californians approved the ban in 1988 (~59%), rejected similar measures in 2000 (Prop 25, ~2:1) and 2010 (Prop 15, 58% no). Current PPIC polling (Oct 2026) shows 45% yes / 52% no — it's one of the weakest measures on the ballot.
- **Sides:** Backed by LWV-CA, Common Cause, CA NORW, and the state Democratic Party; opposed by the California Taxpayers Association, Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, former FPPC chair and commissioners, and multiple editorial boards (SF Chronicle, San Diego Union-Tribune, Mercury News/East Bay Times).

A "no" vote preserves the existing ban and keeps the option of trying a better-designed program in the future.

Proposition 4
Repeals Prohibition Against Public Funding of Election Campaigns. Legislative Statute.
Analysis of Measure
Background
The Political Reform Act. Many people, groups, and businesses spend money to support or oppose candidates for public office and ballot measures. California's Political Reform Act sets rules for how money can be used in politics and requires public reporting of political spending. These rules apply to state and local candidates, ballot measures, and other public officials, but not to federal candidates or officials. (Federal law establishes campaign finance and reporting requirements for federal offices.) The Political Reform Act has been updated by voters over the years.
Ban on Public Funds to Pay for Campaigns. The Political Reform Act bans the use of public funds for political candidates' campaigns. This ban applies to most elected offices at the state level and local level. (This ban does not apply to city office elections in certain charter cities. Los Angeles, San Francisco, Long Beach, Oakland, and Berkeley are current examples of charter cities that provide public funds to certain campaigns.)
Entities That Oversee Campaign Finance Laws. California's campaign finance laws are administered by the Fair Political Practices Commission and the California Secretary of State. State law requires people and groups to report how much money they give, receive, and spend on political campaigns. This information is available to the public on the Secretary of State's website. The Fair Political Practices Commission enforces and interprets the Political Reform Act. The Fair Political Practices Commission reviews the finance reports and can fine candidates and donors who break the law. The Fair Political Practices Commission issues guidance based on its interpretation of the Political Reform Act.
Proposal
Lifts Ban on Use of Public Funds to Pay for Candidates' Campaigns. Proposition 4 lifts the ban on using public funds for political candidates' campaigns. Removing the ban allows state and local governments to create public campaign financing programs in the future if they wish. Proposition 4 does not create a public campaign finance system for the state or local governments directly.
Sets Rules for Future State and Local Public Campaign Finance Programs. Proposition 4 sets broad rules for future state and local public campaign finance programs but leaves many key design decisions to future state and local decision makers. Proposition 4 limits which public funds can be used for campaigns, who can receive the funds, and how the funds can be spent in any future public campaign finance program. For example, money meant for education, transportation, or public safety cannot be used for campaigns. Candidates can only receive public funds if they show broad-based support in their district and agree to spending limits and other program rules. Public funds cannot be used for legal defense fees or fines, or to repay a candidate's personal campaign loan. State and local governments can design and implement their own programs within the broad rules set by Proposition 4.
Fair Political Practices Commission Would Issue Guidance on Public Campaign Finance Programs. Proposition 4 specifies that the Fair Political Practices Commission is not required to administer or enforce local public campaign finance programs. Rather, state and local government officials could ask the Fair Political Practices Commission for guidance on how to create public campaign finance programs consistent with Proposition 4.
Fiscal Effects
Costs of Possible Public Campaign Finance Programs Depend on Future Decisions. Proposition 4 does not create a public campaign finance program. However, it allows state and local governments to create such programs in the future. The cost of these programs could be significant for governments that choose to create them. The total cost would depend on which governments created such programs and how those programs were designed.
Minor State Costs to Support State and Local Governments Considering Public Campaign Finance Programs. If voters approve Proposition 4, state and local government officials likely would ask the Fair Political Practices Commission for guidance on creating public campaign finance programs under the Political Reform Act. This likely would require the Fair Political Practices Commission to hire more legal staff to help answer these questions. As a result, state costs would be a few hundred thousand dollars each year. This amount is much less than one-tenth of 1 percent (0.1 percent) of the state's total General Fund budget. (The General Fund is the account the state uses to pay for most public services, including education, health care, and prisons.)
Yes/No Statement
A YES vote on this measure means: State and local governments could create public campaign financing programs for public office candidates, subject to limits on which public funds could be used, how the public funds could be used, and who could receive them.
A NO vote on this measure means: State and most local governments would remain unable to create public campaign finance programs for public office candidates.
Summary of Legislative Analyst's Estimate of Net State and Local Government Fiscal Impact
Ongoing costs to the state of a few hundred thousand dollars each year for the Fair Political Practices Commission to answer questions from state and local governments about public campaign finance programs.

In summary
Prop. 4 would lift a ban that prohibits state and most local candidates from using public funding for their political campaigns. Proponents argue the mechanism helps more candidates run for office, but opponents are skeptical.
Follow the election results in California: Sign up for our newsletter (https://calmatters.org/subscribe-to-calmatters/california-election-newsletter/) to receive alerts when the contests for governor, Prop. 40, insurance commissioner and other key results are called.
In 1988, a Democrat, a Republican and an independent in the state Legislature co-authored a ballot measure to ban most political campaigns from using public money.
Their rationale? There was already too much money in politics.
“It certainly makes no sense to open the biggest money source of all, the taxpayers’ purses and wallets,” proponents argued (https://repository.uclawsf.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=1988&context=ca_ballot_props). Nearly 60% of voters agreed.
Almost four decades later, some good-government groups argue that the state needs to do the exact opposite to counter the influence of money in politics.
They, along with the state Democratic Party, are backing Proposition 4 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-4-public-fundraising/) on the November ballot, which would lift the 1988 ban and authorize the state and most local governments to set up public campaign financing systems for state and local races.
Seven charter cities in California, including San Francisco, Berkeley and Oakland, were spared from the 1988 ban and already have public campaign financing.
To qualify for the funding, candidates must meet criteria such as proving they have a certain number of small donors or agreeing to cap how much they raise and spend on their campaign. Depending on the city, eligible candidates receive the funding as a grant, a matching fund indexed to their total donations, or a voucher voters can give to campaigns.
Proponents of Prop. 4 may face an uphill battle: Voters have twice rejected similar ballot measures to lift the ban, and public polling so far suggests voters are skeptical.
What supporters, opponents say
Elections have gotten more expensive over the past three decades, both federally and statewide.
In 2000, federal candidates, parties and special interests spent $5.6 billion on congressional and presidential races. By 2020, that number had nearly quadrupled to $18 billion (https://www.opensecrets.org/elections-overview/cost-of-election?display=T), according to OpenSecrets, a Washington, D.C.-based nonprofit that tracks campaign spending nationwide.
In California, special interests spent $26 million (https://calmatters.org/politics/2025/10/prop50-money-ads-mailers-billboards/) running competing ads on redistricting last year, making it the most expensive ballot measure race in state history. This year, California had the most expensive governor’s race (https://www.nytimes.com/2026/06/03/us/elections/california-governor-campaign-finance.html) in U.S. history, with billionaire Tom Steyer pouring $213 million (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/06/california-rich-candidates-funding-elections/) of his own money into his unsuccessful gubernatorial bid.
Supporters of Prop. 4 say public campaign financing is necessary as a check against that kind of unfettered private campaign spending, because candidates often must accept campaign spending limits to qualify for public funding. They say public financing will lead to more diverse candidates by attracting those who otherwise couldn’t afford to run for office.

“We need to change the way we finance election campaigns so candidates can run and win without having to raise big money, and they can spend their time listening to voters rather than their donors,” said Trent Lange, president of California Clean Money Campaign and co-chair of the Yes on Prop. 4 campaign.
Gov. Gavin Newsom (https://calmatters.org/tag/gavin-newsom/) and the Democratic-led state Legislature, which voted last year (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/bills/ca_202520260sb42) to place Prop. 4 on the November ballot, also support the measure. Sen. Tom Umberg (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/legislators/thomas-umberg-165043), a Santa Ana Democrat and a co-author of Prop. 4, said it would help alleviate a “growing cynicism in politics” and allow candidates to spend more time developing policies instead of fundraising.
“To the extent that we can engage particularly small donors, that will … empower and also engage the body politic, particularly young people,” he said.
But opponents say politicians should not use taxpayer dollars (https://caltax.org/prop4/) to run campaigns. They argue the measure would force voters to subsidize candidates they otherwise wouldn’t support, and that fraudulent candidates could exploit the system.
Voters have previously rejected ballot initiatives that would have allowed public money to be used for political campaigns. Nearly two-thirds of voters shot down a 2000 measure that would have allowed candidates to tap public funds for advertising (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2000/25_03_2000.html). In 2010, 58% of voters opposed a 2010 measure (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_15,_Biennial_Lobbyist_Fee_and_Public_Campaign_Funding_Measure_(June_2010)) to lift the 1988 ban.
“The voters have been quite clear they don’t want taxpayer money being used for politics,” Assemblymember Carl DeMaio (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/legislators/carl-demaio-161014), a San Diego Republican, said last year (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/hearings/278290#t=221&f=fe479f37ee7a3df6888379e9be069fd8) on the Assembly floor. “Unfortunately, politicians simply can’t take no for an answer.”

Critics also doubt the effectiveness of Prop. 4, arguing it is not specific enough to have teeth.
Prop. 4 offers only broad instructions to local governments and the state. It would ban candidates from using public funds meant for education, public safety and transportation. It would require candidates to prove they have enough public support and to agree to certain spending limits to receive funding, but doesn’t spell out how much. It would also ban candidates from using the money to pay for legal defenses, fines or personal loans to their campaigns.
The measure specifically exempts the Fair Political Practices Commission, the state’s campaign finance watchdog, from ensuring local programs are not exploited or abused, leaving it largely to local governments. But not every local government has its own watchdog agency, let alone an effective one.
The San Francisco Chronicle’s editorial board, in opposing Prop. 4, argued that its rules “are only meaningful if they’re enforced by independent, nonpartisan bodies. And Prop. 4 offers no guarantee they will be.”
Effectiveness debate
Fifteen states and Washington, D.C., offer some sort of statewide public financing for political campaigns, according to an analysis by the National Conference of State Legislatures (https://www.ncsl.org/elections-and-campaigns/public-financing-of-campaigns-overview).
Studies are mixed on the effectiveness of those programs.
Some, including one in 2003 (https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/1532673X03256784) by two University of Maryland scholars, suggest that candidates who accept public financing spend less time fundraising, freeing them up for other campaign activities.
Some researchers found that public financing expanded the pool of candidates running for office. A 2022 study of Seattle’s program (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0047272722000780), which gives each registered voter four $25 vouchers to contribute to the campaign of their choice, concluded that the program boosted the number of candidates by 86%. Another study (https://web.stanford.edu/~neilm/The%20Impact%20of%20Public%20Financing%20on%20Electoral%20Competition.pdf) of Arizona and Maine’s programs found that they “significantly increased competition.”
Others disagreed. The United States Government Accountability Office, the nonpartisan research agency advising Congress, studied Arizona and Maine’s programs (https://www.gao.gov/assets/gao-10-390.pdf) in 2010 and concluded there was no evidence that public financing led to more candidates.
There’s little evidence that public financing has curbed the influence of private donors, according to the Seattle study and the GAO report.
In California, few studies have examined the effectiveness of local programs. A 2023 San Francisco Ethics Commission study found candidates have increasingly tapped into the public funds and that third-party spending was “at near all-time lows.” But the commission encouraged a more comprehensive analysis. A 2013 study (https://www.oaklandca.gov/files/assets/city/v/3/boards-amp-commissions/documents/pec/publications/reports-by-third-parties/2013-05-01-evaluating-oaklands-limited-public-financing-act.pdf) in Oakland found no evidence its program diluted the influence of wealthy donors, although it did seem to boost competition.
Researchers point to the difficulty (https://sgp.jhu.edu/primers/public-funding-of-us-elections/#conclusion) of studying public financing programs, because most apply in only a handful of states and it is hard to measure what would have happened if the programs had not been in place.
The lack of compelling evidence makes Prop. 4 proponents’ claims shaky, the San Diego Union-Tribune’s editorial board (https://www.sandiegouniontribune.com/2026/09/04/endorsement-dont-buy-prop-4s-baloney-about-publicly-financed-campaigns/) argued.
“So Proposition 4’s only certain effect would be to create a new category of government spending that taxpayers could be required to pay for — one with no track record of delivering promised benefits,” it said.
The ballot measure should not be overly prescriptive, said Dora Rose, deputy director for the League of Women Voters of California, a co-sponsor of Prop. 4.
“Prop. 4 sets basic safeguards and then lets communities learn from the evidence and decide what works for them,” she said.
For now, voters appear skeptical. A September poll (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/) from the Public Policy Institute of California found 53% of likely voters would oppose Prop. 4, while just 42% would vote yes. Another poll (https://escholarship.org/content/qt3w14s99c/qt3w14s99c.pdf) by the UC-Berkeley Institute of Governmental Studies shows a tighter matchup, with 35% of likely voters supporting the measure and another 35% against it.

Should California taxpayers chip in to fund political campaigns? Prop. 4 lets you decide

By Yue Stella Yu, CalMatters

This story was originally published by CalMatters. Sign up for their newsletters.

In 1988, a Democrat, a Republican and an independent in the state Legislature co-authored a ballot measure to ban most political campaigns from using public money. 

Their rationale? There was already too much money in politics. 

“It certainly makes no sense to open the biggest money source of all, the taxpayers’ purses and wallets,” proponents argued. Nearly 60% of voters agreed.

Almost four decades later, some good-government groups argue that the state needs to do the exact opposite to counter the influence of money in politics.

They, along with the state Democratic Party, are backing Proposition 4 on the November ballot, which would lift the 1988 ban and authorize the state and most local governments to set up public campaign financing systems for state and local races. 

Seven charter cities in California, including San Francisco, Berkeley and Oakland, were spared from the 1988 ban and already have public campaign financing. 

To qualify for the funding, candidates must meet criteria such as proving they have a certain number of small donors or agreeing to cap how much they raise and spend on their campaign. Depending on the city, eligible candidates receive the funding as a grant, a matching fund indexed to their total donations, or a voucher voters can give to campaigns.

Proponents of Prop. 4 may face an uphill battle: Voters have twice rejected similar ballot measures to lift the ban, and public polling so far suggests voters are skeptical.

What supporters, opponents say

Elections have gotten more expensive over the past three decades, both federally and statewide. 

In 2000, federal candidates, parties and special interests spent $5.6 billion on congressional and presidential races. By 2020, that number had nearly quadrupled to $18 billion, according to OpenSecrets, a Washington, D.C.-based nonprofit that tracks campaign spending nationwide.

In California, special interests spent $26 million running competing ads on redistricting last year, making it the most expensive ballot measure race in state history. This year, California had the most expensive governor’s race in U.S. history, with billionaire Tom Steyer pouring $213 million of his own money into his unsuccessful gubernatorial bid. 

Supporters of Prop. 4 say public campaign financing is necessary as a check against that kind of unfettered private campaign spending, because candidates often must accept campaign spending limits to qualify for public funding. They say public financing will lead to more diverse candidates by attracting those who otherwise couldn’t afford to run for office. 

“We need to change the way we finance election campaigns so candidates can run and win without having to raise big money, and they can spend their time listening to voters rather than their donors,” said Trent Lange, president of California Clean Money Campaign and co-chair of the Yes on Prop. 4 campaign. 

Gov. Gavin Newsom and the Democratic-led state Legislature, which voted last year to place Prop. 4 on the November ballot, also support the measure. Sen. Tom Umberg, a Santa Ana Democrat and a co-author of Prop. 4, said it would help alleviate a “growing cynicism in politics” and allow candidates to spend more time developing policies instead of fundraising. 

“To the extent that we can engage particularly small donors, that will … empower and also engage the body politic, particularly young people,” he said.

But opponents say politicians should not use taxpayer dollars to run campaigns. They argue the measure would force voters to subsidize candidates they otherwise wouldn’t support, and that fraudulent candidates could exploit the system.

Voters have previously rejected ballot initiatives that would have allowed public money to be used for political campaigns. Nearly two-thirds of voters shot down a 2000 measure that would have allowed candidates to tap public funds for advertising. In 2010, 58% of voters opposed a 2010 measure to lift the 1988 ban.

“The voters have been quite clear they don’t want taxpayer money being used for politics,” Assemblymember Carl DeMaio, a San Diego Republican, said last year on the Assembly floor. “Unfortunately, politicians simply can’t take no for an answer.”

Critics also doubt the effectiveness of Prop. 4, arguing it is not specific enough to have teeth. 

Prop. 4 offers only broad instructions to local governments and the state. It would ban candidates from using public funds meant for education, public safety and transportation. It would require candidates to prove they have enough public support and to agree to certain spending limits to receive funding, but doesn’t spell out how much. It would also ban candidates from using the money to pay for legal defenses, fines or personal loans to their campaigns.

The measure specifically exempts the Fair Political Practices Commission, the state’s campaign finance watchdog, from ensuring local programs are not exploited or abused, leaving it largely to local governments. But not every local government has its own watchdog agency, let alone an effective one.

The San Francisco Chronicle’s editorial board, in opposing Prop. 4, argued that its rules “are only meaningful if they’re enforced by independent, nonpartisan bodies. And Prop. 4 offers no guarantee they will be.”

Effectiveness debate

Fifteen states and Washington, D.C., offer some sort of statewide public financing for political campaigns, according to an analysis by the National Conference of State Legislatures. 

Studies are mixed on the effectiveness of those programs.

Some, including one in 2003 by two University of Maryland scholars, suggest that candidates who accept public financing spend less time fundraising, freeing them up for other campaign activities. 

Some researchers found that public financing expanded the pool of candidates running for office. A 2022 study of Seattle’s program, which gives each registered voter four $25 vouchers to contribute to the campaign of their choice, concluded that the program boosted the number of candidates by 86%. Another study of Arizona and Maine’s programs found that they “significantly increased competition.” 

Others disagreed. The United States Government Accountability Office, the nonpartisan research agency advising Congress, studied Arizona and Maine’s programs in 2010 and concluded there was no evidence that public financing led to more candidates. 

There’s little evidence that public financing has curbed the influence of private donors, according to the Seattle study and the GAO report.

In California, few studies have examined the effectiveness of local programs. A 2023 San Francisco Ethics Commission study found candidates have increasingly tapped into the public funds and that third-party spending was “at near all-time lows.” But the commission encouraged a more comprehensive analysis. A 2013 study in Oakland found no evidence its program diluted the influence of wealthy donors, although it did seem to boost competition. 

Researchers point to the difficulty of studying public financing programs, because most apply in only a handful of states and it is hard to measure what would have happened if the programs had not been in place.

The lack of compelling evidence makes Prop. 4 proponents’ claims shaky, the San Diego Union-Tribune’s editorial board argued.

“So Proposition 4’s only certain effect would be to create a new category of government spending that taxpayers could be required to pay for — one with no track record of delivering promised benefits,” it said. 

The ballot measure should not be overly prescriptive, said Dora Rose, deputy director for the League of Women Voters of California, a co-sponsor of Prop. 4.

“Prop. 4 sets basic safeguards and then lets communities learn from the evidence and decide what works for them,” she said.

For now, voters appear skeptical. A September poll from the Public Policy Institute of California found 53% of likely voters would oppose Prop. 4, while just 42% would vote yes. Another poll by the UC-Berkeley Institute of Governmental Studies shows a tighter matchup, with 35% of likely voters supporting the measure and another 35% against it.

REPEALS PROHIBITION AGAINST PUBLIC FUNDING OF ELECTION CAMPAIGNS. LEGISLATIVE STATUTE.
ARGUMENT IN FAVOR OF PROPOSITION 4
YES ON PROPOSITION 4, THE CALIFORNIA FAIR ELECTIONS ACT: ELECTIONS SHOULD BE WON, NOT BOUGHT
The amount of money in California elections is outrageous; it's distorting our democracy. Since 2020, more than $1 billion has been spent on California state candidate races alone. This massive spending gives special interests greater access and influence while drowning out the voices of ordinary Californians.
PROP. 4 HELPS QUALIFIED CANDIDATES COMPETE
Running for office today often requires either personal wealth or access to wealthy donors. Deep pockets have become an unofficial requirement to run for office, leaving too many qualified candidates behind.
PROP. 4 CHANGES THE WAY WE FINANCE ELECTION CAMPAIGNS
Programs like small-dollar donation matching help candidates compete without relying on wealthy donors. However, most California communities are banned from using these tools, allowing the influence of big money to grow.
Proposition 4 lifts that ban, giving voters and local governments the option to adopt public financing with strict safeguards so qualified candidates-regardless of their income-can compete against candidates who are backed by wealthy interests.
PROP. 4 BUILDS ON A PROVEN MODEL
We know this reform works because it's working in other states. Thousands of candidates from different backgrounds have been elected in fourteen states and 26 localities using similar systems. They are new people with good ideas from all walks of life. Because they don't rely on wealthy donors, they can speak their mind and work for the people, not the special interests.
PROP. 4 GIVES LOCAL COMMUNITIES A CHOICE
Proposition 4 does not create a public financing program. It simply gives local governments the option to adopt one if they choose.
If a community does, the cost is as little as $1 per resident each year-a small investment to help counter the billions spent influencing California's elections.
PROP. 4 PROTECTS TAXPAYERS
Taxpayer Safeguards:
Requires candidates to meet strict eligibility criteria and abide by spending limits to qualify for public funds.
Prohibits public funding from favoring incumbents or discriminating based on political party.
Prohibits the use of public funds for legal defense or fines.
PROP. 4 CRACKS DOWN ON ILLEGAL FOREIGN MONEY
Proposition 4 triples the maximum fines for illegal foreign campaign contributions and expenditures, strengthening penalties for those who attempt to interfere in California's elections.
PROP. 4 IS SUPPORTED BY LEADERS ACROSS CALIFORNIA
Proposition 4 is backed by a broad coalition including League of Women Voters of California, California Nurses Association, Mental Health Advocacy Services, Social Security Works, California Clean Money Campaign, California Common Cause, California National Organization for Women, Californians for Disability Rights, Consumer Watchdog, Courage California, Democracy for America, Indivisible California: Statestrong, La Defensa, Money Out Voters In, Voters Right to Know, and many others.
PROP. 4 GIVES CALIFORNIANS THE OPPORTUNITY TO RECLAIM THEIR ELECTIONS and ensure they reflect the values of the people, not just the wealthiest donors.
YES ON 4-Restore power to voters, not wealthy donors
Lorrel Plimier , Co-President
League of Women Voters of California
Catherine Kennedy , President
California Nurses Association
Tom Umberg , California State Senator
REBUTTAL TO ARGUMENT IN FAVOR OF PROPOSITION 4
Here is what the politicians supporting Proposition 4 do not tell you:
Proposition 4 REPEALS the voter-approved law that PROHIBITS candidates from using taxpayer money to run for office.
Proposition 4 has NO LIMIT on the number of candidates who can get taxpayer money. In the election last June, more than 60 candidates ran for Governor. Proposition 4 would allow thousands of candidates to get taxpayer money!
Proposition 4 has NO LIMIT on how much taxpayer money a candidate can get. Proposition 4 opens the door to taxpayer-funded campaigns but provides no limits on how much taxpayer money a candidate can get and NO LIMIT on spending. It will lead to more negative ads, more junk mail, and more annoying text messages.
Proposition 4 does NOT PROHIBIT SPECIAL INTEREST MONEY in campaigns. Proposition 4 ALLOWS candidates to get taxpayer money AND to get special interest money! Where exactly is the money going to come from to fund thousands of political campaigns? Proposition 4 does not say. But you know the answer. It is coming from YOU, the taxpayers! Less money for schools, less money for public safety, less money for healthcare. More money for politicians.
Proposition 4 is a BLANK CHECK. It is based on false promises and failed solutions.
Proposition 4 does NOT protect taxpayers. That is why Proposition 4 is opposed by California's leading taxpayer organizations.
Proposition 4 does NOT provide for “fair elections.” That is why Proposition 4 is opposed by former Commissioners of the Fair Political Practices Commission.
Vote NO ON PROPOSITION 4.
Robert Gutierrez , President
California Taxpayers Association
Jon Coupal , President
Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association
Dan Schnur , Former Chair
Fair Political Practices Commission
ARGUMENT AGAINST PROPOSITION 4
Why did Sacramento politicians put Proposition 4 on the ballot? They want access to YOUR TAXPAYER MONEY to fund THEIR OWN CAMPAIGNS.
Proposition 4 repeals a voter approved law that PROHIBITS these politicians from using public taxpayer funds for their own campaigns. That's right, Proposition 4 allows politicians to use your taxpayer money to fund their campaigns.
Proposition 4 has NO LIMIT on the number of candidates who can get taxpayer money and NO LIMIT on how much money they can get! Proposition 4 is a BLANK CHECK. There isn't even a limit on how much they can spend on their campaigns! More negative ads. More junk mail. More annoying text messages. More, more, more.
Proposition 4 is so poorly written, it could allow every state or local “candidate” to get public funding. They don't even have to actually qualify for the ballot to get taxpayer money. Proposition 4 allows for public funding of thousands of state and local candidates. It even allows for public financing of candidates for county political party committees.
In just the last primary election, there were more than 60 candidates for Governor. Do you want YOUR TAXPAYER MONEY going to support more of their negative campaign ads and junk mail?
Proposition 4 has NO LIMIT on how much taxpayer money a candidate can receive. It says it requires “strict criteria” to receive taxpayer funds but provides NO DETAILS on what the criteria are! Read the fine print:
“‘Strict criteria' means the requirement set by statute, ordinance, or charter that candidates must meet to receive public funds.”
But there is no current statute, ordinance or charter setting any criteria. Guess who will be setting the criteria? The same politicians who want to get your taxpayer money!
Some good government groups support public financing of campaigns because they want to get special interest money out of politics. BUT PROPOSITION 4 DOES NOT GET RID OF SPECIAL INTEREST MONEY! Under Proposition 4, candidates can raise money from special interests AND get public funding too.
Proposition 4 is the worst kind of public financing scheme. It provides no specifics. It leaves all the details to be worked out by the same politicians who want to get access to public funds.
It is a blank check. But worse than that, Proposition 4 allows special-interest funding of political campaigns.
Please join California's leading taxpayer protection organizations, including the California Taxpayers Association, the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, the Family Business Association of California, United Latinos Action, as well as former members of California's Fair Political Practices Commission, who all oppose Proposition 4.
PLEASE VOTE NO ON THE POLITICIANS' BLANK CHECK PROPOSITION. VOTE NO ON PROP. 4.
Dan Schnur , Former Chair
Fair Political Practices Commission
Colleen McAndrews , Former Commissioner
Fair Political Practices Commission
Julian Canete , President
California Hispanic Chambers of Commerce
REBUTTAL TO ARGUMENT AGAINST
PROPOSITION 4
DON'T BE MISLED BY SPECIAL INTERESTS WHO WANT TO KEEP BUYING ELECTIONS
California is the ONLY state that bans public funding of campaigns. Communities in all 49 other states have the right to adopt public financing to allow qualified candidates to compete against wealthy donors. California doesn't. Prop. 4 simply removes that ban and gives local voters the same choice everyone else has, while instituting strict taxpayer safeguards.
PROP. 4 GIVES POWER BACK TO LOCAL COMMUNITIES AND EMPOWERS VOTERS, NOT DONORS
Prop. 4 doesn't spend a single taxpayer dollar or institute public financing anywhere. It simply removes the ban to give every city, county, and the state the right to adopt public funding if local voters want it. The details are appropriately left to each community. But any system MUST require candidates to abide by spending limits and demonstrate broad-based support in their district to qualify.
PROP. 4 MAKES ELECTED OFFICIALS ACCOUNTABLE TO VOTERS, NOT DONORS
Corporate special interests oppose Prop. 4 because public financing allows candidates to run and win without relying on them-threatening their grip on California elections.
Thousands of candidates from different backgrounds have been elected across the country using public financing, for a tiny cost. Because they don't rely on wealthy donors, they can speak their minds and work for the people, not special interests.
DON'T BE FOOLED BY CORPORATE SPECIAL INTERESTS HIDING BEHIND NICE-SOUNDING NAMES.
VOTE YES ON 4 to let local voters and communities reclaim their elections so they're won, not bought.

At this point, I have a pretty good grasp of the situation. Let me check a bit more: the expert endorsements (from Ballotpedia or similar sites), the editorial board recommendations, and whether there's any independent expert analysis backing one side or the other. Also, let me check the details of the proposed bill text itself and the details of SB 42.

Main considerations:

Arguments in favor of voting YES:
1. It doesn't actually spend any taxpayer money right now — it just authorizes state and local governments to create programs in the future (optionality, local control).
2. It includes safeguards: cannot use funds from education, transportation, or public safety; candidates must demonstrate broad-based support; spending limits; cannot use funds for legal defense, fines, or personal loans; cannot discriminate by party or incumbent status.
3. California is the only state that still maintains a ban on public campaign financing.
4. Backed by the League of Women Voters of California, Common Cause, CA NORW, Consumer Watchdog, and others.
5. Aims to counter the influence of big money (Steyer's $213 million in the 2026 gubernatorial race).
6. Trips up foreign interference by tripling the maximum fines on foreign contributions.

Arguments in favor of voting NO:
1. Voters have rejected similar measures twice before (Prop 25 in 2000, Prop 15 in 2010) — the ban was voter-approved in 1988 (roughly 59% of voters).
2. Current polling: 53% opposition vs 42% support (PPIC); in IGS, 35% support vs 35% opposition.
3. The measure is too vague — "strict criteria" is undefined, no cap on the amount of money, no cap on the number of candidates; details left to the politicians themselves.
4. The state-level watchdog (FPPC) is explicitly excluded from enforcing local programs.
5. Evidence on effectiveness is mixed: GAO found no increase in the number of candidates; little evidence of a reduction in donor influence.
6. Editorial boards (SF Chronicle, San Diego Union-Tribune) oppose.
7. Opponents include the California Taxpayers Association, Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, and a former FPPC chair.

The LAO (nonpartisan) analysis is neutral: it doesn't create a program; costs are a few hundred thousand dollars per year for FPPC; future costs depend on local decisions.

Considerations:
- This measure is largely an authorization/permission, not an obligation. No new spending is mandated.
- The main criticism is that it leaves details to future politicians, with weak enforcement mechanisms, and that evidence of effectiveness is mixed.
- The main criticism from the opposition side is the "blank check" framing, but the LAO notes that nothing is mandated.
- Historical precedent: California voters have rejected similar measures in 1988 (the ban), 2000 (Prop 25, rejected by roughly 2-to-1), and 2010 (Prop 15, 58% opposition). This suggests that California voters have expressed a consistent, informed view that public funds should not be used for campaigns. The 1988 ban was explicitly voter-approved.
- Current polling also leans toward opposition (53 to 42).

Hmm, but polling and past votes are not necessarily grounds for my recommendation; they're just data points about voter sentiment. The question is, based on my research, which is the better policy choice.

Let me think about what a careful, evidence-based recommendation would look like:

For YES:
- Low-risk, low-cost (a few hundred thousand dollars per year)
- Preserves local control/optionality
- The current ban is an outlier — only California bans this
- Potential benefits: more diverse candidates, reduced reliance on wealthy donors
- Safeguards are built in

For NO:
- Repeals a voter-approved ban (1988)
- Rejected twice before by similar measures
- Weak enforcement design (the watchdog is excluded)
- Vague criteria = future politicians set the rules
- Evidence that it achieves its goals is mixed to negative (GAO)
- The "spending limits" requirement may actually have little effect, since the funds can coexist with private fundraising — that is, it may just add public funds on top of private funds, increasing overall spending rather than reducing donor influence
- Editorial boards oppose

Actually, one important point to verify: does the proposal allow candidates to receive public funds while also raising private funds? The "against" argument says, "Prop. 4 permits candidates to get special interest money AND public funds." Let me check the actual bill text. If candidates who take public funds can also keep private fundraising, then the core reform mechanism (spending limits as a substitute for private funds) is undermined — the public funds simply become an additive subsidy, increasing total spending. This is a substantive policy weakness.

PROPOSED LAW
SECTION 1. This act shall be known, and may be
cited, as the California Fair Elections Act of 2026.
SEC. 2. The Legislature finds and declares all of the
following:
(a) All citizens should be able to make their voices
heard in the political process and hold their elected
officials accountable.
4 (b) Elections for local or state elective office should be
fair, open, and competitive.
(c) The increasing costs of political campaigns can
force candidates to rely on large contributions from
wealthy donors and special interests, which can give
those wealthy donors and special interests
disproportionate influence over governmental
decisions.
(d) Such disproportionate influence can undermine
the public’s trust that public officials are performing
their duties in an impartial manner and that government
is serving the needs and responding to the wishes of all
citizens equally, without regard to their wealth.
(e) Special interests contribute more to incumbents
than challengers because they seek access to elected
officials, and such contributions account for a large
portion of the financial incumbency advantage, as
confirmed by studies such as those published in the
Journal of Politics in 2014 and Political Research
Quarterly in 2016.
(f) Citizen-funded election programs, in which
qualified candidates can receive public funds for the
purpose of communicating with voters rather than
relying exclusively on private donors, are currently
operative in five charter cities in California, as well as
numerous other local and state jurisdictions.
(g) Citizen-funded election programs encourage
competition by reducing the financial advantages of
incumbency and making it possible for citizens from all
walks of life, not only those with connections to wealthy
donors or special interests, to run for office, as
confirmed by studies such as those published in State
Politics and Policy Quarterly in 2008, and by the
Campaign Finance Institute in 2015, the National
Institute on Money in State Politics in 2016, and the
State Politics and Policy Quarterly in 2022.
(h) By reducing reliance on wealthy donors and special
interests, citizen-funded election programs inhibit
improper practices, protect against corruption or the
appearance of corruption, and protect the political
integrity of our governmental institutions.
(i) In Johnson v. Bradley (1992) 4 Cal.4th 389, the
California Supreme Court highlighted the Court of
Appeal’s observation that “it seems obvious that public
money reduces rather than increases the fund raising
pressures on public office seekers and thereby reduces
the undue influence of special interest groups.”
116 | Text of Proposed Laws
(j) In Buckley v. Valeo (1976) 424 U.S. 1, the United
States Supreme Court recognized that “public
financing as a means of eliminating the improper
influence of large private contributions furthers a
significant governmental interest.”
(k) In Arizona Free Enterprise v. Bennett (2011) 564
U.S. 721, the United States Supreme Court
acknowledged that public financing of elections “can
further ‘significant governmental interest[s]’ such as
the state interest in preventing corruption,” quoting
Buckley v. Valeo.
(l) In Buckley v. Valeo, the United States Supreme
Court further noted that citizen-funded elections
programs “facilitate and enlarge public discussion and
participation in the electoral process, goals vital to a
self-governing people.”
(m) The absolute prohibition on public campaign
financing allows special interests to gain
disproportionate influence and unfairly favors
incumbents. An exception should be created to permit
citizen-funded election programs so that elections may
be conducted more fairly.

85300. (a) Except as provided in subdivision (b), a A

by any state or local entity for education, transportation,
or public safety.
(b) A public officer or candidate may expend or accept
public moneys for the purpose of seeking elective office
if the state or a local governmental entity establishes a
dedicated fund for this purpose by statute, ordinance,
resolution, or charter, and both of the following are
true:
(1) Public moneys held in the fund are available to all
qualified, voluntarily participating candidates for the
same office without regard to incumbency or political
party preference.
(2) The state or local governmental entity has
established criteria for determining a candidate’s
qualification by statute, ordinance, resolution, or
charter.
(b) Candidates shall abide by expenditure limits and
meet strict criteria to qualify for public funds.
(c) Public funds shall not be utilized to pay legal
defense fees or fines.
(d) (1) A candidate shall not, at any time, use public
funds to repay a personal loan to their campaign.
(2) A candidate who receives public funds for their
campaign shall not, after their campaign ends, use any
source of funds to repay a personal loan to their
campaign.
(e) For purposes of this section, the following
definitions apply:

(1) “Available candidate funds” means the candidate’s
expenditure limit or the sum of all contributions and
public funds received by the candidate’s controlled
committee for the elective office, whichever is less.
(2) “Expenditure limits” means voluntary spending
limits established by statute, ordinance, or charter that
qualified, voluntarily participating candidates must
abide by to receive public funds.
(3) “Independent expenditures against” means the
sum of any expenditures made or expenses incurred by
any person or persons for the purpose of making
independent expenditures in opposition to a specific
candidate.
(4) “Independent expenditures in support” means the
sum of any expenditures made or expenses incurred by
any person or persons for the purpose of making
independent expenditures in support of a specific
candidate.
(5) “Net supportive funds” means the sum of available
candidate funds, plus the independent expenditures in
support of that candidate, minus the independent
expenditures against that candidate.
(6) “Public funds” means any moneys provided to a
candidate by a state or local governmental entity for the
purpose of seeking elective office.
(7) (A) “Strict criteria” means the requirements set by
statute, ordinance, or charter that candidates must
meet to receive public funds. These criteria shall require
candidates to demonstrate broad-based support in their
district, such as by requiring candidates to receive
small-dollar contributions or vouchers from a specified
number of voting-age residents.
(B) (i) If a statute, ordinance, or charter requires a
minimum number of individuals making small-dollar
contributions pursuant to subparagraph (A), the largest
contribution the statute, ordinance, or charter may
require for a contributor to be counted is ten dollars
($10).
(ii) For purposes of this subparagraph, a statute,
ordinance, or charter may allow a contribution larger
than the small-dollar contribution amount required
pursuant to subparagraph (A) to be counted as a
contribution equal to the small-dollar contribution
amount required pursuant to subparagraph (A).
(C) “Strict criteria” shall not include requirements that
candidates receive a specified number of signatures or
raise a specified total dollar amount of more than ten
dollars ($10) per contributor.
(f) (1) A statute, ordinance, or charter may increase
the expenditure limits for each qualified, voluntarily
participating candidate.
(2) An increased limit pursuant to this subdivision shall
not exceed an amount equal to the highest dollar
amount of net supportive funds of any other candidate
for the same office, plus the dollar amount of
independent expenditures against the qualified,
voluntarily participating candidate, minus the dollar
amount of independent expenditures in support of the
qualified, voluntarily participating candidate.
(g) Public funding statutes, charters, ordinances, and
resolutions shall not discriminate based on party or
according to whether a candidate is a challenger or an
incumbent.
(h) The Commission is not responsible for the
administration or enforcement of a system of public
funding of candidates established by a local
governmental agency.
(i) Subdivisions (e), (f), and (h) of this section may be
amended by statute pursuant to subdivision (a) of
Section 81012. The remaining subdivisions of this
section may be amended only by a statute that complies
with subdivision (b) of Section 81012.

Proposition 4: Repeals Prohibition Against Public Funding
Proposition 4: Repeals Prohibition Against Public Funding
Proposition 4: Repeals Prohibition Against Public Funding of Election Campaigns. Legislative Statute.
Additional Titles
Public Fundraising, Allow Public Financing of Election Campaigns Measure
Summary
Proposition 4 was placed on the ballot by Senate Bill 42 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260SB42) (SB 42). SB 42 changes provisions of the Political Reform Act of 1974, which bans the use of public funds for candidates’ political campaigns. The senate passed the bill in June 2025, with the Assembly passing it in September 2025. Gov. Gavin Newsom signed the bill in October, sending it to the ballot as Proposition 4.
Proposition 4 would remove California’s prohibition on using public money to finance political candidates, allowing state and local governments to establish publicly funded campaign programs in the future. The measure would not itself create such a program, but would give governments the option to develop their own systems within statewide guidelines.
Under the measure, funds dedicated to purposes such as education, transportation, and public safety could not be redirected to campaigns. Candidates receiving public financing would have to demonstrate a sufficient level of support among voters and comply with spending limits and other program requirements. Public funds could not be used for legal defense costs, fines, or repayment of a candidate’s personal campaign loans. State and local governments would determine the details of their individual programs, while the Fair Political Practices Commission (https://www.fppc.ca.gov/) could provide guidance on complying with Proposition 4 but would not be required to administer or enforce local programs.
F iscal Impact
(Summary of Legislative Analyst's Estimate of Net State and Local Government Fiscal Impact)
Proposition 4 would not automatically require new spending because it does not establish a public campaign financing program. Costs would arise only if the state or local governments later choose to create such programs, with the amount depending on how widely they are adopted and how they are structured. The state would also likely spend a few hundred thousand dollars annually for additional Fair Political Practices Commission (https://www.fppc.ca.gov/) staff to advise governments on developing programs that comply with the measure.
What your vote means
Yes: A “yes” vote would end the statewide ban on public campaign financing, allowing state and local governments to establish programs that provide public funds to qualifying candidates under specified rules and spending limits.
No: A “no” vote would maintain the existing prohibition on public financing of campaigns, including the current exception for certain charter cities.

Pro/Con Statements
Pro Con
Supporters argue that Proposition 4 would reduce the influence of wealthy donors and special interests by allowing state and local governments to establish public campaign financing programs. They say these programs could help qualified candidates compete for office without relying heavily on wealthy donors, while requiring participating candidates to meet eligibility requirements and spending limits. Proposition 4 would also prohibit using funds earmarked for education, transportation, or public safety and would strengthen penalties for illegal foreign campaign contributions.
Opponents argue that Proposition 4 could allow taxpayer money to be used to fund political campaigns without setting specific limits on how much public funding candidates could receive. They contend that important details are not included, leaving many key decisions to future state and local decision makers. Critics note that candidates receiving public funds could still accept private and special-interest contributions, meaning the measure would not eliminate private money from campaigns.
